pages.title: Change the conditions, change the product

blocks.text: Ordinary HBr addition to propene mainly gives 2-bromopropane, but HBr with suitable peroxide conditions mainly gives 1-bromopropane. The substrate is unchanged; a different reaction mechanism changes the preferred orientation.

We use that contrast to understand the peroxide effect, then connect alkene addition with hydration, oxidation, ozonolysis and polymerisation. Each transformation uses the π bond differently, so identify reagents and work-up before predicting products.

pages.transition: The change in orientation begins with a different radical chain.

pages.title: Peroxide begins a radical chain

blocks.text: Peroxides can undergo homolysis and generate radicals. In the HBr radical chain, Br• adds to a double bond and creates a carbon radical. The carbon radical then takes hydrogen from HBr, giving product and regenerating Br•. This differs from forming a carbocation first.

For propene, Br• + CH3CH=CH2 → CH3CH•CH2Br; then CH3CH•CH2Br + HBr → CH3CH2CH2Br + Br•. The first step places the radical on the more substituted middle carbon, helping explain why Br attaches to the terminal carbon.
A carbonyl group contains C=O. An aldehyde has at least one H on its carbonyl carbon, whereas a ketone has carbon groups on both sides of that carbon.

pages.transition: That chain explains both the peroxide product and the limits of the effect.

pages.title: Anti-Markovnikov has a specific scope

blocks.text: The major peroxide-mediated product of propene with HBr is 1-bromopropane, opposite to ordinary ionic orientation. The practical peroxide effect applies to HBr; the corresponding radical chains with HCl or HI do not have both necessary propagation steps energetically favourable.

Do not extend “anti-Markovnikov” automatically to every reagent or alkene reaction. Peroxide is not consumed once per product molecule as though it supplied bromine. It initiates a radical pathway; the hydrogen and bromine incorporated in the product come from HBr.

pages.transition: Water and acids add through another set of stated conditions.

pages.title: Acid addition and hydration

blocks.text: Cold concentrated H2SO4 can add across an alkene to give an alkyl hydrogen sulphate. Acid-catalysed addition of water gives an alcohol; simple unsymmetrical alkenes follow the usual Markovnikov orientation in this elementary treatment.

Propene hydration is CH3CH=CH2 + H2O → CH3CH(OH)CH3 with suitable acid catalysis. The product is propan-2-ol. H and OH add across the double bond; the acid assists the mechanism and is regenerated rather than being included as a permanent group in this hydration product.

pages.transition: An oxidant can add oxygen-containing groups instead of H and halogen.

pages.title: Gentle oxidation adds two hydroxyl groups

blocks.text: Cold, dilute alkaline or neutral permanganate oxidises an alkene to a vicinal diol, also called a glycol: the two –OH groups lie on neighbouring carbons. The purple permanganate colour disappears as it is reduced, an observation used in testing unsaturation.

Ethene gives HOCH2CH2OH under these conditions. Both carbons of the original C=C become alcohol-bearing carbons. The observation is useful but is not an absolute proof of one unique structure, since other readily oxidised substances can also affect a permanganate test.

pages.transition: More vigorous oxidation can break the carbon skeleton completely at C=C.

pages.title: Strong oxidation can split the carbon skeleton

blocks.text: Vigorous oxidation cleaves C=C rather than merely forming a diol. Product identity depends on the groups attached to each double-bond carbon: a carbon carrying H can be oxidised to a carboxylic acid, while a carbon carrying two carbon groups gives a ketone. Terminal carbon may be oxidised further to CO2.

But-2-ene gives two ethanoic-acid fragments under suitable strong oxidative conditions. Each C=C carbon originally has one H and one CH3. The statement identifies the organic products; a fully balanced redox equation additionally depends on the oxidant and reaction medium.

pages.transition: Ozonolysis makes that cleavage particularly useful for locating the double bond.

pages.title: Ozonolysis reveals the position of C=C

blocks.text: Ozonolysis adds ozone to an alkene and cleaves the original double bond after work-up. With reductive work-up such as Zn/H2O, each double-bonded carbon becomes a carbonyl carbon. A carbon originally bearing H gives an aldehyde; one bearing two carbon groups gives a ketone.

CH3CH=CHCH3 gives two CH3CHO molecules on reductive ozonolysis. Cut the C=C into two halves and replace each end with C=O while keeping its attached CH3 and H. The equal ethanal fragments identify the symmetrical position of the original double bond.

pages.transition: Working backwards from carbonyl fragments turns the reaction into a structure tool.

pages.title: Reconstruct an alkene from its fragments

blocks.text: Suppose reductive ozonolysis gives methanal, HCHO, and propanone, (CH3)2CO. Remove the carbonyl oxygens conceptually and join the two carbonyl carbons with C=C. The reconstructed structure is CH2=C(CH3)2, 2-methylpropene. Check that its four carbon atoms equal the combined product carbons.

This is a structure deduction, not a claim that mixing the two carbonyl products reverses ozonolysis. Work-up matters: oxidative conditions may convert aldehydes further to acids. Name the work-up before using the aldehyde/ketone fragment rule.

pages.transition: A different use of π bonding links many alkene units into a polymer.

pages.title: Many small molecules become one chain

blocks.text: Polymerisation joins many monomer molecules into a high-molecular-mass polymer. Addition polymerisation of ethene opens its π bonds and links the carbon units into a chain. No small molecule needs to be eliminated in this idealised addition scheme.

n CH2=CH2 → [–CH2–CH2–]ₙ under suitable catalyst, temperature and pressure conditions. The bracketed pair of carbon atoms is the repeating unit of polyethene. n counts the number of monomer units, not the number of carbon atoms in a single ethene molecule.

Teacher-created structure check: pent-2-ene gives ethanal and propanal on reductive ozonolysis. Their carbon counts, two plus three, recover five. A different work-up can oxidise the aldehydes, so always preserve the stated work-up when comparing your prediction with experimental products.

pages.transition: The reagents and work-up now distinguish these several outcomes clearly.

pages.title: Read the conditions before the product

blocks.text: Ordinary HBr addition and peroxide-mediated HBr addition follow different ionic and radical pathways. Hydration gives an alcohol, mild permanganate gives a vicinal diol, and strong oxidation can cleave C=C. These are different outcomes of reacting the same functional bond.

Reductive ozonolysis turns each C=C carbon into a carbonyl carbon and can locate the double bond. Addition polymerisation turns monomers into repeating chain units. Preserve reagent, work-up, atom counts and the distinction between overall product patterns and fully balanced redox equations.

questions.question: What is the major propene + HBr product with suitable peroxide conditions?
questions.answer: 1-Bromopropane, formed by the radical pathway with anti-Markovnikov orientation.

questions.question: Should the peroxide effect be assumed for HCl addition?
questions.answer: No. The useful peroxide effect in this treatment is specific to HBr; the analogous HCl and HI propagation steps are not both favourable.

questions.question: What does cold dilute permanganate form from ethene?
questions.answer: Ethane-1,2-diol, HOCH2CH2OH, with hydroxyl groups on the two originally double-bonded carbons.

questions.question: Which alkene gives only ethanal on reductive ozonolysis?
questions.answer: But-2-ene, CH3CH=CHCH3, gives two ethanal molecules per alkene molecule.

questions.question: Reconstruct an alkene giving methanal and propanone on reductive ozonolysis.
questions.answer: Join the carbonyl carbons to obtain CH2=C(CH3)2, 2-methylpropene.

questions.question: Does polyethene retain a C=C in every repeating unit?
questions.answer: No. The monomer π bonds are used to form the chain; the ideal repeating unit is –CH2–CH2–.
